subtopics.name: Relative Basicity of Ammonia, Ethylamine & Phenylamine

parts.problem_md:
4-methylphenylamine can be manufactured from methylbenzene in two steps.

Draw the skeletal formula of the intermediate organic compound formed in step 1.
parts.solution_md:
The skeletal formula of the intermediate is:

![Skeletal formula of 1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene, showing a benzene ring with a methyl group at position 1 and a nitro group (NO2) at position 4](assets/001-skeletal-formula-of-1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene-show.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct skeletal formula of 1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene

> **[exam-tip]**
> To prepare an aromatic amine, the benzene ring must first be nitrated to introduce a –NO<sub>2</sub> group, which is then reduced to –NH<sub>2</sub> in the second step.
> 
> The methyl group on methylbenzene directs the incoming electrophile to the ortho and para positions. The para product, 1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene, is the major product due to steric factors.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

4-methylphenylamine can be manufactured from methylbenzene in two steps.

State the reagents and conditions required for step 1.

reagents ...............................................................

conditions ...............................................................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reagents and conditions for step 1 are:
> 
> - Concentrated nitric acid / conc HNO<sub>3</sub>
> **AND**
> concentrated sulfuric acid / conc H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / reflux between 30–50 °C **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A nitrating mixture of concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> and concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> generates the nitronium ion (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>), which acts as the electrophile in the electrophilic substitution reaction.
> 
> Because the methyl group activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution, nitration of methylbenzene requires a lower temperature than for plain benzene (55 °C). A temperature of 30–50 °C achieves mono-nitration while reducing the risk of a di-nitrated product forming.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

4-methylphenylamine can be manufactured from methylbenzene in two steps.

Step 2 involves heating the intermediate under reflux with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid.

Explain why aqueous sodium hydroxide must also be added to obtain 4-methylphenylamine.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Sodium hydroxide is required because:
> 
> - The reduction in strongly acidic conditions produces the protonated amine / 4-methylphenylammonium salt rather than the free amine **[1 mark]**
> - Aqueous sodium hydroxide deprotonates the ammonium salt / acts as a base to neutralise the acid and liberate the free amine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When the nitro group is reduced using Sn and concentrated HCl, the acidic conditions immediately protonate the –NH<sub>2</sub> group as it forms, producing a 4-methylphenylammonium salt. The nitrogen's lone pair accepts H<sup>+</sup> from the acid.
> 
> To obtain the free amine, aqueous NaOH is added after the reduction step. It accepts the H<sup>+</sup> from the ammonium ion (acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base), releasing the neutral 4-methylphenylamine.

parts.problem_md:
The azo dye 4-hydroxyazobenzene, C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>10</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O, can be produced from phenylamine as shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Reaction scheme for the synthesis of 4-hydroxyazobenzene from phenylamine: phenylamine reacts in step 1 to form benzenediazonium chloride, which undergoes coupling in step 2 to form 4-hydroxyazobenzene](assets/002-reaction-scheme-for-the-synthesis-of-4-hydroxyaz.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

Step 1 requires nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>, which is generated in situ.

i) State the reagents and conditions required for step 1.

reagents ...............................................................

conditions ...............................................................

[2]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction that takes place in step 1.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions required for step 1 are:
> 
> - NaNO<sub>2</sub> / sodium nitrite
> **AND**
> HCl / dilute hydrochloric acid **[1 mark]**
> - Temperature below 10 °C / ice / ice-cold conditions **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for step 1 is:
> 
> - C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HNO<sub>2</sub> + HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O
> **OR**
> C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + NaNO<sub>2</sub> + 2HCl → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> + NaCl + 2H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) is unstable and must be generated in situ by mixing sodium nitrite (NaNO<sub>2</sub>) with dilute hydrochloric acid immediately before use.
> 
> The temperature condition (below 10 °C) is for the stability of the diazonium salt product, not for the formation of nitrous acid. Above 10 °C, the diazonium ion rapidly decomposes by reacting with water to form phenol and nitrogen gas.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The azo dye 4-hydroxyazobenzene, C~12~H~10~N~2~O, can be produced from phenylamine as shown in Fig. 3.1.

Reaction scheme for the synthesis of 4-hydroxyazobenzene from phenylamine: phenylamine reacts in step 1 to form benzenediazonium chloride, which undergoes coupling in step 2 to form 4-hydroxyazobenzene

Step 2 is a coupling reaction.

State the name of the organic reagent required to react with benzenediazonium chloride to form 4-hydroxyazobenzene.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The organic reagent is:
> 
> - Phenol / C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> 4-hydroxyazobenzene contains an –OH group on one of the aromatic rings, which originates from phenol, the coupling partner. Phenol is dissolved in alkaline conditions (NaOH (aq)) to form the more reactive phenoxide ion (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sup>−</sup>) before coupling.
> 
> A common error is to suggest a compound that already contains nitrogen. The diazonium salt provides both nitrogen atoms in the –N=N– azo group. The coupling reagent simply needs to be an electron-rich aromatic compound activated by an electron-donating group such as –OH or –NR<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 3.2 shows the structure of another azo dye.

![Structure of a methyl orange analogue azo dye, showing two aromatic rings connected by an N=N azo linkage with an N-methylphenylamine fragment on one ring](assets/003-structure-of-a-methyl-orange-analogue-azo-dye-sh.png)

**Fig. 3.2**

State the systematic name of the secondary amine used to form the structure shown in Fig. 3.2.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The systematic name of the secondary amine is:
> 
> - *N*-methylphenylamine **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To identify the secondary amine, examine the nitrogen-containing fragment on the coupling half of the azo dye in Fig. 3.2. The nitrogen is bonded to a methyl group and a phenyl ring.
> 
> The secondary amine has the structure CH<sub>3</sub>–NH–C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, which is *N*-methylphenylamine. It is also called methylaniline; aniline is the common name for phenylamine (aminobenzene).

parts.problem_md:
The acid-base indicator methyl red is an azo dye synthesised from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and phenylamine. Fig. 1.1 shows the first stages of this synthesis.

![Synthesis scheme for methyl red showing: 2-nitrobenzaldehyde undergoes step 1 (oxidation) to give 2-nitrobenzoic acid, then step 2 (reduction) to give compound A (2-aminobenzoic acid), which undergoes step 3 (diazotization) and coupling with phenylamine to give methyl red](assets/004-synthesis-scheme-for-methyl-red-showing-2-nitrob.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the reagents and conditions for steps 1 and 2 of the synthesis.

step 1 ...............................................................

step 2 ...............................................................

[3]

ii) Draw the structural formula of compound **A** in the box provided. The nitrogen-containing group must be shown fully displayed.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reagents and conditions for steps 1 and 2 are:
> 
> Step 1:
> 
> - Potassium / sodium dichromate(VI) / K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> / Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
> **AND**
> sulfuric acid / H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> / H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Heat / reflux **[1 mark]**
> 
> Step 2:
> 
> - Tin / Sn
> **AND**
> concentrated HCl / hydrochloric acid
> **AND**
> heat / heat under reflux **[1 mark]**

ii) Correct structures for compound **A** include:

| ![Skeletal formula of 2-aminobenzoic acid showing a benzene ring with a carboxylic acid group at position 1 and an amino group (NH2) at position 2](assets/005-skeletal-formula-of-2-aminobenzoic-acid-showing-.png) | ![Skeletal formula of the protonated form of 2-aminobenzoic acid showing an ammonium group (NH3 positive) with the carboxylic acid group](assets/006-skeletal-formula-of-the-protonated-form-of-2-ami.png) | ![Skeletal formula of 2-aminobenzoic acid hydrochloride salt showing the protonated ammonium group and Cl minus counterion](assets/007-skeletal-formula-of-2-aminobenzoic-acid-hydrochl.png) |
|---|---|---|

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct structure of 2-aminobenzoic acid (–NH<sub>2</sub> and –COOH groups at ortho / adjacent positions on the benzene ring)
> 
> 1 mark for –NH<sub>2</sub> group fully displayed (both H atoms shown on the N atom)
> 
> Allow the protonated ammonium form or hydrochloride salt form

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step 1 oxidises the aldehyde group (–CHO) of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde to a carboxylic acid (–COOH) using acidified dichromate(VI). This is the standard aldehyde to carboxylic acid oxidation.
> 
> Step 2 reduces the nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) to an amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>) using tin and concentrated HCl under reflux. Compound A is 2-aminobenzoic acid (also known as anthranilic acid).
> 
> Since the reduction is carried out in strongly acidic conditions, compound A initially forms as the protonated ammonium salt or hydrochloride salt. All three structural forms are accepted.

parts.problem_md:
When heated, phenylamine reacts with iodomethane to form compound **B**, *N*-methylphenylamine.

i) Describe the mechanism for the formation of the *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt from the reaction of phenylamine and iodomethane. Include all relevant curly arrows, lone pairs, and dipoles.

[3]

ii) A further reaction occurs with an excess of iodomethane to form compound **C**, *N,N*-dimethylphenylamine.

Explain what this implies about the relative basicity of phenylamine and compound **B**.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
i) The mechanism for the formation of the *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt is:

![Mechanism diagram showing nucleophilic substitution: the lone pair on the N atom of phenylamine attacks the delta positive carbon of iodomethane while the C-I bond breaks heterolytically, forming N-methylphenylammonium iodide salt with positive charge on N and I minus as a separate species](assets/008-mechanism-diagram-showing-nucleophilic-substitut.jpg)

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for curly arrow from the lone pair on N of phenylamine to the δ+ carbon of iodomethane
> 
> 1 mark for curly arrow from the C–I bond to the I atom
> 
> 1 mark for correct product showing positive charge on the N atom **AND** I<sup>−</sup> / iodide ion as a separate species

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction. Phenylamine (the nucleophile, lone pair on N) attacks iodomethane (the electrophile, δ+ on C):
> 
> - One curly arrow from the lone pair on N to the δ+ carbon of CH<sub>3</sub>I
> - One curly arrow from the C–I bond to I
> - Product: *N*-methylphenylammonium iodide salt with positive charge on N and I<sup>−</sup> as a separate ion

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) This implies about the relative basicity:
> 
> - Compound **B** / *N*-methylphenylamine is a stronger base than phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> - The methyl group in compound **B** donates electron density towards the N atom / positive inductive effect of the methyl group **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in compound **B** is therefore more available to accept a proton than in phenylamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> Both compounds contain a phenyl ring, so the delocalising effect of the ring on the N lone pair applies equally to both. The only structural difference is the methyl group in compound **B**.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Since both phenylamine and compound **B** contain the phenyl ring, the delocalisation of the N lone pair into the π system applies equally to both. The only difference is the methyl group in compound **B**, which donates electron density towards N (positive inductive effect), making the lone pair more available to accept H<sup>+</sup>. This makes compound **B** a stronger base, which explains why excess iodomethane is required to form compound **C**.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The acid-base indicator methyl red is an azo dye synthesised from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and phenylamine. Fig. 1.1 shows the first stages of this synthesis.

Synthesis scheme for methyl red showing: 2-nitrobenzaldehyde undergoes step 1 (oxidation) to give 2-nitrobenzoic acid, then step 2 (reduction) to give compound A (2-aminobenzoic acid), which undergoes step 3 (diazotization) and coupling with phenylamine to give methyl red

Explain why the temperature used in step 3 must be kept between 0 °C and 10 °C.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The temperature must be kept between 0 °C and 10 °C because:
> 
> - Above 10 °C, the diazonium salt decomposes / reacts with water / forms a phenol / nitrogen gas is evolved **[1 mark]**
> - Below 0 °C, the reaction rate is too slow / the diazotization does not proceed at a practical rate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 0–10 °C range is a compromise between two competing requirements:
> 
> - The upper limit (below 10 °C) prevents the diazonium salt from decomposing. Above this temperature the N–N<sup>+</sup> group leaves as nitrogen gas and the diazonium ion reacts with water to form a phenol derivative, destroying the intermediate before it can be used.
> - The lower limit (above 0 °C) ensures the reaction proceeds fast enough to be practical.
> 
> This temperature constraint applies to any diazotization step in diazonium salt chemistry.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 1.2 shows the structure of indigotin. It can be synthesised from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and propanone in aqueous sodium hydroxide.

![Structural formula of indigotin, a blue dye with a symmetric bicyclic structure containing two indole units connected by a C=C double bond, with NH and C=O groups](assets/009-structural-formula-of-indigotin-a-blue-dye-with-.png)

![Skeletal formula of indigotin showing the two fused ring systems connected by a central C=C bond](assets/010-skeletal-formula-of-indigotin-showing-the-two-fu.png)

**Fig. 1.2**

i) Complete the equation for this reaction, shown in Fig. 1.3.

![Incomplete equation for the synthesis of indigotin from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and propanone in aqueous NaOH, with blank spaces for balancing coefficients and products](assets/011-incomplete-equation-for-the-synthesis-of-indigot.png)

**Fig. 1.3**

[1]

ii) Calculate the mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde required to produce 12.0 g of indigotin from this reaction. The percentage yield is 82.0%. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
i) The completed equation is:

![Balanced equation for the synthesis of indigotin from 2 molecules of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and 2 molecules of propanone in aqueous NaOH, giving indigotin plus 2 sodium ethanoate and water](assets/012-balanced-equation-for-the-synthesis-of-indigotin.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct balancing: 2 propanone + 2 NaOH; products include 2 CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> and H<sub>2</sub>O

> **[exam-tip]**
> Propanone (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>, 3 carbons) contributes one carbon to each of the two five-membered rings in indigotin. Two propanone molecules are needed, each losing a CH<sub>3</sub> group that becomes sodium ethanoate (CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>). Balance NaOH and water last.

ii) To calculate the mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde required:

- Find *M*<sub>r</sub> values:

*M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = (7 x 12) + (5 x 1) + 14 + (3 x 16)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = 151 g mol<sup>−1</sup>

*M*<sub>r</sub> of indigotin = (16 x 12) + (10 x 1) + (2 x 14) + (2 x 16)

*M*<sub>r</sub> of indigotin = 262 g mol<sup>−1</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Find theoretical mass and moles of indigotin (100% yield):

mass at 100% yield = $\frac{100}{82.0} \times 12 . 0$

mass at 100% yield = 14.63 g

moles of indigotin = $\frac{14.63}{262}$

moles of indigotin = 0.05585 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Find mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde:

molar ratio 2 : 1 from equation

moles of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = 0.05585 x 2

moles of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde = 0.1171 mol

mass = 0.1171 x 151

mass = **17.7 g**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the *M*<sub>r</sub> of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde **AND ** indigotin
> 
> 1 mark for the moles of indigotin
> 
> 1 mark for the mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect *M*<sub>r</sub> value in subsequent steps

> **[exam-tip]**
> The 82.0% yield means 12.0 g is only 82.0% of the theoretical maximum. Scale up first (12.0 ÷ 0.820 = 14.63 g), then use *M*<sub>r</sub> and the 2 : 1 molar ratio to find the mass of starting material.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 1.4 shows the structure of Coumarin 440.

![Reaction scheme showing the structure of Coumarin 440 with blank boxes for the structures of compounds D and E](assets/013-reaction-scheme-showing-the-structure-of-coumari.png)

![Reaction scheme for Coumarin 440 transformations showing labelled blank product boxes for D and E](assets/014-reaction-scheme-for-coumarin-440-transformations.png)

**Fig. 1.4**

Coumarin 440 is hydrolysed with excess aqueous sodium hydroxide to form organic compound **D**.

Coumarin 440 reacts with ethanoyl chloride to form organic compound **E**.

Draw the skeletal formulae of compounds **D** and **E** in the boxes provided.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
The skeletal formulae of compounds **D** and **E are:**

Compound **D**:

![Alternative representation of compound D as the sodium salt form of the hydrolysis product](assets/015-alternative-representation-of-compound-d-as-the-.png)

Compound **E**:

![Either accepted structure for compound E alongside the Coumarin 440 starting material for comparison](assets/016-either-accepted-structure-for-compound-e-alongsi.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the structure of compound **D**, with hydrolysed ester linkage with carboxylate and phenoxide groups shown as deprotonated anions (–O<sup>−</sup> / –COO<sup>−</sup>), consistent with excess NaOH conditions
> 
> 1 mark for the structure of compound **E**, showing an amide bond (–NHCOCH<sub>3</sub>) formed from condensation of the amine group with ethanoyl chloride

> **[exam-tip]**
> Compound **D** (hydrolysis with excess NaOH):
> 
> The excess NaOH has two effects:
> 
> - It hydrolyses the lactone (cyclic ester) ring, opening the ring to give a hydroxy acid
> - The excess base then deprotonates both the carboxylic acid and phenolic –OH groups, giving the di-anion / sodium salt form
> 
> Compound **E** (condensation with ethanoyl chloride):
> 
> - Ethanoyl chloride (CH<sub>3</sub>COCl) reacts with the –NH<sub>2</sub> group of Coumarin 440 in a nucleophilic addition-elimination reaction
> - The N lone pair attacks the carbonyl carbon; HCl is eliminated; amide bond –NHCOCH<sub>3</sub> forms
> - If there are two –NH<sub>2</sub> groups, both may react to give the double condensation product
> 
> Tip: draw Coumarin 440 as a general R–NH<sub>2</sub> molecule to make it easier to identify the product:

parts.problem_md:
Three nitrogen-containing molecules, ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, and *N*-methylethanamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NHCH<sub>3</sub>, are drawn below in Fig. 1.1.

![Three amine molecules: ammonia (NH3), phenylamine (C6H5NH2), and N-methylethanamine (CH3CH2NHCH3), shown as structural diagrams](assets/017-three-amine-molecules-ammonia-nh3-phenylamine-c6.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

i) State the relative order of basicity of the three amine molecules shown in Fig. 1.1.

least basic ......................... < ......................... < ......................... most basic

[1]

ii) Explain your answer to part (i).

[4]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The relative order of basicity, from least to most basic, is:
> 
> - Phenylamine < ammonia < *N*-methylethanamine **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The explanation for the order of basicity is:
> 
> - Alkyl groups donate electron density towards the N atom in *N*-methylethanamine / the methyl and ethyl groups have a positive inductive effect **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in *N*-methylethanamine is more available to accept a proton / bond with H<sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - In phenylamine, the lone pair on N overlaps with / becomes delocalised into the π system of the benzene ring **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair on N in phenylamine is therefore less available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Base strength depends on the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen atom to accept H<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> For *N*-methylethanamine: two alkyl groups donate electron density towards N through the positive inductive effect, making the lone pair more available. This makes it the strongest base of the three.
> 
> For phenylamine: N is bonded directly to the benzene ring. The lone pair overlaps with the delocalised π electron system, partially withdrawing it from N and reducing its availability to bond with H<sup>+</sup>. This makes phenylamine the weakest base, weaker even than ammonia, which has no interaction with an aromatic ring system.

parts.problem_md:
Phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, can be produced from nitrobenzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NO<sub>2</sub>.

State the name of the type of reaction and the reagents and conditions required for this conversion.

type of reaction ...............................................................

reagents ...............................................................

conditions ...............................................................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The type of reaction and the reagents and conditions are:
> 
> - Type of reaction: Reduction **[1 mark]**
> - Reagents: Tin / Sn
> **AND**
> concentrated HCl / hydrochloric acid **[1 mark]**
> - Conditions: Heat / heat under reflux
> **AND**
> NaOH (aq) / sodium hydroxide solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The conversion of nitrobenzene to phenylamine is a core syllabus reaction involving reduction of the nitro group (–NO<sub>2</sub>) to an amino group (–NH<sub>2</sub>).
> 
> The tin and concentrated HCl reduce the nitrobenzene under heat. The strongly acidic conditions produce a phenylammonium salt rather than the free amine. Aqueous sodium hydroxide is then added to deprotonate the salt and release phenylamine.

parts.problem_md:
Phenylamine, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, can be used in the manufacture of azo dyes. In the first step, phenylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid and nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>, to form a diazonium salt.

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> + HCl + HNO<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

In the second step, the diazonium salt solution is added to an alkaline solution of a phenol coupling agent to form the azo dye.

i) The diazonium salt, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup>, is unstable. State the essential temperature condition required to prevent the diazonium salt from decomposing during this reaction.

[1]

ii) Draw the structure of the diazonium salt formed in this reaction. The nitrogen-containing group must be shown fully displayed.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The essential temperature condition is:
> 
> - Below 10 °C / between 0 °C and 10 °C / ice-cold conditions **[1 mark]**

ii) The structure of the diazonium salt is:

![Structural formula of benzenediazonium chloride, showing a phenyl group bonded to two nitrogen atoms connected by a triple bond, with a positive charge on the terminal N atom and Cl minus as the counterion](assets/018-structural-formula-of-benzenediazonium-chloride-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct N≡N<sup>+</sup> triple bond AND positive charge on the terminal N atom AND Cl<sup>−</sup> counterion

> **[exam-tip]**
> The diazonium salt must be kept below 10 °C at all times. Above this temperature it decomposes. The N<sub>2</sub> group leaves as nitrogen gas, and the diazonium ion reacts with water to form phenol, destroying the intermediate before it can be used in the coupling reaction.
> 
> The nitrogen-containing group in the diazonium ion is –N≡N<sup>+</sup>. The two nitrogens are connected by a triple bond, with the positive charge on the terminal N atom furthest from the benzene ring. The counterion is Cl<sup>−</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Phenylamine, C6H5NH2, can be used in the manufacture of azo dyes. In the first step, phenylamine reacts with hydrochloric acid and nitrous acid, HNO2, to form a diazonium salt.

C6H5NH2 + HCl + HNO2 → C6H5N2+Cl− + 2H2O

In the second step, the diazonium salt solution is added to an alkaline solution of a phenol coupling agent to form the azo dye.

In the second step of azo dye production, the diazonium salt reacts with an alkaline solution of a phenol coupling agent.

Draw the skeletal formula of the azo dye formed if the coupling agent used is 2,6-dimethylphenol.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
The skeletal formula of the azo dye is:

![Skeletal formula of the azo dye formed from benzenediazonium chloride and 2,6-dimethylphenol, showing two aromatic rings connected by an N=N azo linkage, with the diazonium ring attached at the para position of the 2,6-dimethylphenol ring and the OH group retained](assets/019-skeletal-formula-of-the-azo-dye-formed-from-benz.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct –N=N– azo linkage connecting the two aromatic rings
> 
> 1 mark for coupling at the 4-position (para to –OH) of the 2,6-dimethylphenol ring, with –OH group retained

> **[exam-tip]**
> In 2,6-dimethylphenol, the methyl groups at positions 2 and 6 block both ortho positions relative to –OH. The coupling reaction therefore occurs at the para position (position 4).
> 
> A common error is to draw the azo linkage at an ortho position, which is sterically impossible when both ortho positions are occupied by methyl groups.
